The fifth installment of Er Mu’s translation of Trevor Cox’s Now You’re Talking turns from hearing to speaking. When did language arise? Estimates range from about 70,000 to 700,000 years ago, depending on whether only Homo sapiens could speak, or Neanderthals and even Homo heidelbergensis too.

Cox explains the voice as source and filter. The vocal folds buzz at about 200 Hz in women and 110 Hz in men, and the vocal tract’s resonances, the formants, shape vowels; Clint Eastwood’s monotone and the vocoded vocals of ELO and Daft Punk show that formants alone carry the words. Compared with chimpanzees, we have a lowered larynx and no air sacs. The larynx descends between three months and four years of age, letting the tongue shape mouth and throat independently, and Philip Lieberman’s pencil-tapping demonstration shows how efficiently speech packs in information. The “supervowel” in “see” helps listeners gauge a speaker’s vocal-tract length.

The fossil evidence points to an early start. Ignacio Martínez estimated from 530,000-year-old neck vertebrae that Homo heidelbergensis had a vocal tract like a ten-year-old child’s, and Tecumseh Fitch’s simulation of a macaque vocal tract produced an intelligible, Gollum-like “Will you marry me?” So why did the larynx drop? Lower formants make a speaker sound bigger, which explains boys’ second descent at puberty. Bart de Boer’s Plexiglas models show air sacs blur vowels; their loss means our vocal tract could support fluent speech at least 500,000 years ago.

Translated into Chinese by Er Mu (edited by Er Mu and Fanyu Meng) from Trevor Cox’s Now You’re Talking: Human Conversation from the Neanderthals to Artificial Intelligence (2018). About the book.
